title: AI Sovereignty and Global Interdependence: Navigating Industry Realities
text:
AI Sovereignty and Global Interdependence: Navigating Industry Realities

Roundtable Summary

October 8th, 2026

On August 12, 2026, Asia Society Policy Institute, New Delhi convened a roundtable discussion titled “AI Sovereignty and Global Interdependence: Navigating Industry Realities.” The discussion, which was organized in partnership with the JSW School of Public Policy at the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIM – A), was held against the backdrop of India's growing investments in semiconductors and AI data centers, as well as the growing debate on AI governance and regulation.The roundtable was conducted under the Chatham House Rule. What follows are the summary, analysis, and key recommendations from the discussion.Summary of the DiscussionAs global economic activities are becoming dependent on digital platforms like e-commerce and social media, countries around the world are attempting to control and manage artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure to establish resilient domestic AI ecosystems. As of 2025, the global digital economy occupies 17.3% of the total global GDP. Further, a 2025 International Data Center Authority survey asserts that approximately 87% of the global industry considers AI as a top priority, highlighting active integration of AI into global businesses. This demonstrates the importance of AI in the global economy, which contributes to each country’s pursuit of sovereign AI. However, attempts to have total control over the AI value chain are futile since it is not controlled by any single country. For example, the Netherlands has dominance over lithography machines, Taiwan dominates the global market share of logic chips, South Korea has market dominance over memory chips, and the United States and China lead in the design of chips and foundation models. Accordingly, establishing resilient AI ecosystems requires cautious management of the international AI value chain that includes capacities such as data centers, capabilities such as talent, and resources such as critical minerals and data. This results in an “AI sovereignty–interdependence paradox,” where AI sovereignty implies complete control over the AI infrastructure value chain, and interdependence implies the AI value chain relies on the capabilities, capacities, and resources of multiple countries.Experts at the roundtable highlighted that for India, this paradox is optimally navigated when AI sovereignty is defined as a maintaining strategic autonomy instead of having a complete control over the AI value chain. Strategic autonomy is achieved by leveraging strengths and building mutually beneficial dependencies with global partners. For India to gain such strategic autonomy, New Delhi should invest in capacity building—data repositories, application development, and talent retention—supported by patient capital with the aim of long-term gains in innovation and scientific break-through. This approach is supported by India’s Chief Economic Advisor Dr. Ananth Nageswaran and Ms. Debjani Ghosh, Chief Architect of Frontier Tech Hub at NITI Aayog, the Indian government’s policy think tank.Since India does not have capabilities in AI infrastructure, semiconductor fabrication, or critical minerals, it must use its institutional capacity for AI governance to gain its strategic autonomy. India already has an architecture for AI governance, as proposed in its AI governance guidelines announced in November 2025. Accordingly, this architecture consists of the AI Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG) and Technology Policy Expert Committee (TPEC), along with AI Safety Institute (AISI) which is operated in a hub-and-spoke model, where different institutions and universities conduct research on AI safety according to their expertise, instead of relying on a single institution. These three bodies provide the skeleton structure for AI governance, which most other countries currently lack. This structure benefits India because it delegates interministerial coordination functions to the AIGEG, institutional functions and technical advisory to TPEC, and AI safety research to the relevant institutions (AISI) in India. This mechanism allows emerging powers like India to take informed measures on AI governance with input from the industry and academia, ensuring AI fuels economic growth and innovation. To leverage this governance architecture, India must further develop it into a globally interoperable governance framework, rather than making it a harmonized framework. Harmonization implies uniform frameworks across jurisdictions, while interoperability can preserve the capacity of the state to modify the architecture in response to the domestic social challenges of AI.To build such an interoperable AI governance framework, one suggestion offered was for New Delhi to consider developing AI governance frameworks through plurilateral institutions. For example, India aligns on AI governance issues with BRICS partners differently than with OECD or G7 frameworks. The 2025 G7 leader’s statement on AI for Prosperity advocates for AI diffusion by enabling cross-border data flows and developing a catalogue of AI solutions. However, the 2025 BRICS leader’s statement emphasizes United Nations centrality in global AI governance while supporting national sovereignty. It should be understood that the push for AI diffusion through the G7 will meet the challenge of AI sovereignty and governance anchored on domestic legislations from BRICS members.BRICS does not contest AI diffusion but instead emphasizes the development of interoperable data governance, AI regulations, and ethical and trustworthy AI while removing barriers to AI access promoting and sustainable development. Therefore, developing a BRICS framework for AI governance may yield more durable outcomes than pursuing universal standards. The 2025 BRICS leaders’ statement advocated for interoperable ICT standards and Global South representation, indicating BRICS nations’ inclination towards developing an interoperable framework for AI governance. Experts at the ASPI-JSW roundtable, in reiterating the interoperable ICT standards, agreed that it is beneficial to consider the existing set of ISO standards like 42001:2023 as the base standard catering to model-level gains and to then build multi-tiered, sectoral standards as per the non-model level gains of an AI system. At the BRICS Summit held in New Delhi on September 12-13, 2026, the members of the bloc unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, advocating for strengthening global AI governance frameworks.To enable interoperable AI governance framework, roundtable participants identified two factors: cross-border data sharing framework and liability regimes. Data sharing will enable the building blocks of AI by providing developers access to diverse datasets, while liability regimes provide legal certainty for compliance and helps to delineate the responsibilities across the final AI value chain. Development of the latter should be the focus of India’s AI Safety Institute, which should further coordinate with other countries’ respective national AISI or equivalent institutions.Navigating the Paradox Starts with Cross-Border Data SharingTo make AI systems interoperable, the treasure trove on which they are built—data—should also be interoperable. Governments have population scale datasets, which, when effectively used, could develop contextual AI systems. A national policy enabling classification and profiling of common datasets should be developed, with global interoperability as a core mandate. India’s National Data Governance Framework, which provides a platform to access standardized government datasets, is a leading example of such a national policy. Although India has a national data governance policy, its implementation is a challenge since data governance (the data generated by the state governments or under the control of state governments) is a sub-national subject, where states or provinces are empowered to design data governance and sharing policies, making it a challenge to bring uniform data sharing practices nationwide.Discussants also advocated for datasets linked to defense and critical infrastructure to be stored in air-gapped data centers, which de-links the model and the data from the internet and therefore restricts access to few approved authorizations. With the exception of critical systems, nonpersonal data should be openly accessible through Application Programming Interfaces (API), making it a nationally provided artifact. India can pioneer such an initiative by bringing this to plurilateral institutions.Developing Legal Certainty Through Liability RegimesDiscussants reconfirmed that defining liability regimes is a top priority for the government. For example, India’s AI Governance Guidelines explicitly outlines the requirement of a graded liability framework, where responsibility is assigned as per the function performed and due diligence undertaken. Recently, Singapore’s Ministry of Law issued a consultation paper on AI and intellectual property regime, indicating that a liability framework will be defined very soon. These developments demonstrate the urgency of forging legal certainty through liability regimes, which was also flagged during the roundtable discussion. Accordingly, India should invest in creating a clear liability regime that brings certainty to business operations, which ultimately enables interoperability and transnational operations of AI companies.Operationalizing the Navigation of Paradox Through AI Safety InstitutesTo ensure interoperable AI governance frameworks, which is a way to navigate the sovereignty-interdependence paradox, India's AISI has an institutional opportunity to position itself as the primary safety institute for the Global South. The Institute’s value lies in generating certifications on data standards and governance frameworks across the AI lifecycle that are calibrated to the needs of emerging economies. However, apart from the projects awarded to various institutions under the Safe & Trusted AI pillar of India AI Mission, the institutional function of AISI remains unclear. Notably, while the director post for India's AISI was announced on May 19, 2026, the position remains vacant as of October 7, 2026, leading to slow progress on technical deliverables of AI safety research. The roundtable discussants noted that the institutional legitimacy of AISI and its active contributions are essential to develop Asia-wide compatible AI governance frameworks.ConclusionIndia's AI governance model is being developed at a moment when global frameworks are diverging rather than converging, as demonstrated by different approaches such as the European Union’s AI Act, China’s World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), Singapore’s AI Verify, and the private sector led approach of the United States. The 2026 AI Impact Summit in New Delhi made clear that India's governance institutions now need to make a durable, straightforward governing principle: sovereignty in AI is not built solely by self-sufficiency; it is built by strategic autonomy providing the capacity to engage with global AI ecosystems on terms that preserve India's regulatory discretion. Choosing interoperability over harmonization is what makes that possible.Accordingly, the 2026 BRICS Chennai Consensus shows that BRICS nations are moving towards AI ecosystem development that leverages complementary strengths of member countries. One example is the working group on High Performing Computing (HPC) and AI and the BRICS submarine cable network, indicating the possibility of the group’s collaboration in the development of AI infrastructure. If the working group on HPCs could reach a consensus on designing a mechanism to create a shared access to HPCs, it would enable AI diffusion at an increased pace. As such, the BRICS submarine cable network, with its own maintenance vessels and access to logistics infrastructures and ports across its member nations, will then be able to reduce the response time of the maintenance vessels to fix the damages caused to the undersea cables. Apart from these working groups focusing on the infrastructure, there was no reference to the interoperability of AI Safety Institutes, cross-border data sharing, or liability regime for AI, which would have been a practical step towards achieving a base-line AI governance framework for the BRICS countries. The 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration explicitly mentions the how bloc would support the 2025 BRICS Leaders' Statement on the Global Governance of Artificial Intelligence, but it falls short on any new initiatives or progress since 2025.
